items.summary_html:
Pacific Press/Getty; Getty Images; Tyler Le/BI

Among New York City's wealthiest homeowners, the stages of grief over the city's hotly contested "pied-à-terre tax" go something like this: First, anger at the chaotic rollout. Then denial, as they pepper lawyers and tax advisors with various versions of "How can they do this?" Bargaining follows, as they hunt for loopholes or long-forgotten documents to plead their cases.

Some can afford to jump straight to the final stage: acceptance. The uber-elite may brush off the new tax, levied on second homes worth at least $5 million, as merely another line item tacked onto their vast portfolios. For most others, however, coming to terms with Mayor Zohran Mamdani's new policy will be more of a journey.

"People do not like hearing the word 'tax,'" Steven Cohen, a longtime luxury real estate agent, tells me.

Those hoping to sidestep the extra bill are running into a big problem: The new tax leaves little daylight for the kinds of workarounds that rich, absentee property owners are floating to their trusted advisors.

"People are trying to get a little creative," says David Fitzhenry, a local real estate attorney who advises high-net-worth clients. "But the way the statute is written, there's not a lot of room for creativity."

Add in the fact that New York City bureaucrats are famously aggressive in chasing down residents whose travel schedules could expose them to the city's steep income tax, and you're looking at a bunch of crestfallen millionaires and billionaires.

"I have one client who said, 'Well, they don't know that I live in Florida,'" recalls Fitzhenry. "I said, 'Where do you file your tax returns?' He says, 'In Florida.'"

Fitzhenry chuckles. "That's a tough sell."

Attorneys and accountants have been fielding concerned calls from wealthy homeowners since mid-April, when Mamdani strode in front of the ultra-luxe condo tower at 220 Central Park South — the site of a $238 million penthouse owned by hedge fund tycoon (and noted Miami resident) Ken Griffin — and reiterated his pledge to "tax the rich." Wringing more dollars from the cushy, largely empty crash pads that dot the five boroughs has long been a point of fascination among those who believe the wealthy should contribute a few more coins to the city's coffers. Previous stabs at a second-home tax, most notably in 2019, gained some traction but ultimately fizzled. This time, though, Mamdani and Gov. Kathy Hochul had the juice: In May, the state legislature passed an annual "pied-à-terre tax" on pricey New York City properties whose owners don't use them as their primary residence.

Citadel CEO Ken Griffin paid a record $238 million for the penthouse at 220 Central Park South.

Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images

For the first couple of years, the tax will apply to one-, two-, and three-family homes worth more than $5 million, as well as condos and co-ops valued by the city at more than $1 million. One important detail: The city has a formula for valuing condos and co-ops that estimates how much income they could generate as rentals and then uses that number to calculate a total dollar figure. These wonky city valuations typically amount to a fraction of the true market value, meaning that a condo valued by the city at $1 million could very well fetch five times that amount in a sale.

For such high-dollar domiciles, even a modest tax can yield a hefty haul. Griffin, for instance, could shell out an extra $1.3 million to $1.4 million next year for his three New York City holdings, my Business Insider colleagues calculated. The mayor's office has said it expects the tax to bring in about $500 million annually.

The rollout this summer spurred another round of angst and recrimination. First, the city began sending ominous letters to thousands of homeowners, warning that they may be subject to the additional bill. Then came an easily searchable list of more than 900,000 New York City properties, along with their owners and valuations. Though the list merely cobbled together already publicly available data, it did make it easier for anyone to ogle their neighbors' homes, and it stoked plenty of outrage among those caught up in its swirl — including many New York residents who won't actually be on the hook for the tax.

"They're really angry," Andrew Jagoda, a real estate attorney, says of some of his clients. "Less sometimes about the tax, though there's certainly that, but about how the city went about doing it and how embarrassed they are."

A lawsuit filed in early August by three New York City homeowners briefly halted the process, but the city quickly appealed, and the rollout continues as the case works its way through the courts (a formal hearing is scheduled for later this month). Notably, the lawsuit doesn't challenge the underlying statute, and the dozen advisors I spoke with say they're telling clients to proceed as if the city will eventually collect its due. "Clients should be prepared for the worst here," Fitzhenry tells me.

The private-jet-setting crowd is used to playing a game of cat and mouse with cities and states eager to claim their fair share of income. The rich meticulously track their time spent in various locations to make sure they don't hit the number of days that could put them on the hook for, say, New York taxes, while on the other side, government employees pore over cellphone records and credit card statements to see if they can make a case to the contrary. This battle can lead globetrotters to embrace some goofy yet indispensable tricks of the trade: installing phone apps that warn when they're approaching resident status, for example, or strategically planning trips so they spend as little time as possible physically present in New York to stay under the 184-day threshold. "Every day counts," says Marisa Friedrich, a New York-based tax advisor. "Even if you're arriving super late on a Monday, you fly in at 11 p.m. — you just created a day for yourself in New York."

Rich property owners who have spent years deftly steering clear of New York income taxes now find themselves in the crosshairs of a different type of levy. Even longtime New Yorkers may get hit with the pied-à-terre surcharge. As the name would suggest, you only get one primary residence, which means that you could live full-time in the city and still face the extra bill if you own multiple properties about town — a fact that has come as a shock to some proud (and wealthy) residents.

"There is a lot of confusion and anger and surprise all built into one for each of these taxpayers," Friedrich tells me. "I don't think anyone that I've spoken to can say that they're happy about it."

The mayor's office has said it expects the pied-à-terre tax to yield about $500 million annually.

Gary Hershorn/Getty Images

There's a simple way for property owners to dodge the tax in the future: fill the apartment. If an immediate family member is living in the home, or if it's leased to a tenant who treats it as their primary residence, then there is no extra bill. If the place is owned by an LLC and the majority stakeholder lives there, it's also in the clear. There's a similar exemption for a home owned through a trust, another common arrangement, if it's occupied by the trust's sole beneficiary.

So let's say you live in Florida but keep a plush Manhattan penthouse valued by the city at $5.3 million (I know, but stick with me here). If you're looking to wriggle out of the additional levy — in this case, more than $340,000 on top of your regular property-tax bill — you've got a handful of options. You could have one of your adult children relocate there, or invite your sister to move in. You could rent the place out to a fellow high-flyer willing to pay tens of thousands of dollars a month in rent. If you want to merely save a few bucks, you could protest your property's valuation and see if the city will knock down its assessment. Maybe you ditch Florida in favor of the Big Apple, though that would likely come with a bigger tax hit, since you'd be subjecting yourself to New York income taxes. Or, of course, you could sell. And that's… sort of it.

"There's not going to be a whole bunch of clever ideas on how to beat it," Fitzhenry tells me.

A bogus lease spun up simply to avoid the tax likely won't pass muster with the city — it has to be an "arm's length" deal, which means you can't have your friend say they live there and charge them $1 a month. In a similar vein, your cousin can't step in and save the day by moving in — immediate family members only. And you can imagine why none of the viable options would sound all that appetizing to someone with enough in their bank account to have a penthouse to their name.

There's not going to be a whole bunch of clever ideas on how to beat it.David Fitzhenry, New York-based attorney

"You have to keep in mind, most of these people are not mom-and-pop," Jagoda tells me. They're not paying off a mortgage and raising kids in that home like most Americans — they just want a nice place in the city where they can come and go as they please. "You're talking about very wealthy people who have a variety of assets worth far more than this," Jagoda adds. Ellen Sykes, a longtime real estate agent, offers a similar assessment of her clients, many of whom own homes in the $4 million to $8 million range. "They're not pleased. They're going to try and find a workaround," Sykes tells me. "But they can afford it, so they're not terrified."

Among the roughly 17,000 who received letters warning they could be on the hook for the tax, many are arguing that the property in question is, in fact, their primary residence. Once the city flags a home as a potential candidate for the pied-à-terre tax, the burden is on the owner to prove otherwise. Jagoda says he has a few clients who are rifling through filing cabinets, searching for decades-old documents that outline the ownership structure and can prove the property qualifies for an exemption. Those who find themselves in this camp are "pissed off," Jagoda tells me. "They have to do this because the way the city set it up, you're guilty until proven innocent."

One thing these lawyers, accountants, and real estate agents aren't buying into: the threatened New York City exodus. The rich may talk a big game about pulling up stakes when their tax bills swell, but there's a lot to keep them owning — and spending — in the city. "It's similar to during COVID when they said, 'Oh, everyone's leaving,'" Cohen, the real estate agent, tells me. "Everyone didn't leave." The exceptions, he notes, are those who might have already had one foot out the door. So far, he says, only one of his clients is selling due to the tax. Even then, they'd already been talking about offloading the property, which they'd used only a handful of times in roughly eight years.

"They can well afford it, but they also don't want to be wasting money, either," Cohen tells me.

For purposes of this year's tax bill, most of this is a moot point — the city is making determinations based on a property's status as of January 5, 2026. Any maneuvers to avoid the tax will, at best, apply to the following year's bill. And while the options for property owners to sidestep the tax may be limited, plenty still find themselves in weird gray areas: Say they've been renovating their primary residence for the past year and living elsewhere, or are stuck sorting out the details of particularly complicated estate planning, like a house owned by an LLC that is then held by a trust. Those types of multi-tiered structures may not work under a strict reading of the rules, Max Biedermann, a New York-based lawyer, tells me, leaving some owners to appeal to reason rather than to law. Co-ops present another thorny situation: While the city may calculate the additional tax for individual units, the entire building gets hit with the extra bill. It's up to the co-op's board to then collect from individual pied-à-terre owners.

"All these other people are getting hit with shrapnel," says Eric Wohl, an attorney who specializes in advising co-op boards.

While there's still plenty of mess to sort out — and thousands of property owners still fuming at the new mayor — it appears that the new tax will be fairly successful in carrying out the mission laid out by Mamdani in the shadow of Ken Griffin's penthouse back in April.

"Yes, it's totally a nuisance," Jagoda concedes. "But it's easier than fighting City Hall."

James Rodriguez is a correspondent on Business Insider's Discourse team.

items.title: WhatsApp Adds Multiple Passkeys, Alphanumeric Passwords, and Caller Context in Security Update
items.summary: Meta has introduced three new security features for WhatsApp . Users can now add more than one passkey to their account, upgrade their two-step verification PIN to a longer alphanumeric password, and see more information about calls from unknown numbers. Meta says that over a billion people use passkeys on WhatsApp. The new passkey and password options are available in the app's account settings. Meta describes these updates as additional ways to secure accounts alongside WhatsApp's default end-to-end encryption. WhatsApp Adds Multiple Passkeys and Stronger Two-Step Verification A passkey allows users to log into WhatsApp using a fingerprint, Face ID, or screen lock code. Meta calls this the fastest and most secure way to verify identity without needing codes or PINs. More than a billion people have set up a passkey. Users can now add multiple passkeys to their account. This is helpful for anyone who uses both Android and iOS devices. To set up a passkey, go to Settings, then Account, then Passkeys. Two-step verification adds another layer of protection against account takeover, even if someone gets your one-time passcode. Previously, this used a six-digit PIN. Meta has replaced the PIN with a longer password that can include letters, numbers, and special characters. This makes it harder to guess. Meta recommends that anyone using a simple PIN like "123456" switch to a stronger password. WhatsApp Adds More Caller Context for Unknown Numbers When a call comes in from a number not saved in contacts, WhatsApp now shows extra information to help users decide whether to answer. On Android, users will now see more information about a non-contact caller, including whether the number is from a different country and whether they have any groups in common. Meta notes that scammers rely on urgency, and the added context lets users pause before answeThese new features are available in WhatsApp settings:tings: Add one or more passkeys by going to Settings, then Account, then Passkeys. This is useful for people who use both Android and iOS. Upgrade two-step verification from a six-digit PIN to a longer password with letters, numbers, and special characters. On Android, check the extra caller information on calls from unknown numbers before deciding to answer. The passkey and two-step verification updates are available in WhatsApp's account settings. The new caller context feature is currently for Android, and there is no information yet about iOS support. Meta has not shared a rollout schedule, so the updates may appear gradually for users. items.title: Quoting Paul Dix
items.summary: The fact that AI wrote 1M LOC and then refined it over the course of the next couple of months to produce a reliable piece of software that is currently running on millions of developer machines is absolutely mind blowing. And you can say, “well it’s not that impressive because they had an oracle to compare against, so it was simple to go from one language to another”, but I think that’s selling this entire thing short. If you can build a verification system and give proper direction, AI can produce a highly complex, highly sophisticated piece of software and it can continue to refine it until it just works. — Paul Dix , The end of programming Tags: coding-agents , ai-assisted-programming , generative-ai , bun , ai , llms
items.summary_html:
The fact that AI wrote 1M LOC and then refined it over the course of the next couple of months to produce a reliable piece of software that is currently running on millions of developer machines is absolutely mind blowing. And you can say, “well it’s not that impressive because they had an oracle to compare against, so it was simple to go from one language to another”, but I think that’s selling this entire thing short. If you can build a verification system and give proper direction, AI can produce a highly complex, highly sophisticated piece of software and it can continue to refine it until it just works.

— Paul Dix, The end of programming

items.title: Apple Announces M6 Mac mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio Aimed at Local AI Workloads and Mac Clustering
items.summary: Apple has introduced two new chips and updated its desktop lineup with the M6 Mac mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio. Both are aimed at local AI workloads and Mac clustering. The M6 is Apple's first chip built on a 2nm process, while the M5 Ultra is the company's first quad-die design and now its most powerful chip. There are no major new features, but both models come with higher specifications and increased prices. Most versions will be available starting September 22, with preorders already open. The 512GB memory option is set to ship in late October. Every performance claim comes from Apple, using its typical "up to" wording against varying baselines. Apple's M6 and M5 Ultra Chip Upgrades The M6 uses TSMC's 2nm process and is the first Apple chip to include all three types of CPU cores in one design. It features 12 CPU cores: two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores. While super cores first appeared in the M5 Pro and M5 Max earlier this year, the M6 is the first to combine all three core types in a single chip. Apple claims the "world's fastest" single-threaded performance, 1.2x the multithreaded throughput of the M5, and 40% faster CPU performance than the M4. The GPU moves to 12 cores with a Neural Accelerator in each, which Apple says delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The chip includes a dual 16-core Neural Engine, storage rated at twice as fast at 15GB/s, and up to 170GB/s of memory bandwThe M5 Ultra stands out as the more notable chip. It uses Apple's UltraFusion interconnect to combine two dual-die M5 Max chips into a single quad-die package. This design provides inter-die bandwidth above 4.4TB/s and over six times the connection density of the previous version. All four dies function as a single processor.e four dies behave as one processor. This setup allows for up to 36 CPU cores, with 12 super cores and 24 performance cores, as well as up to 80 GPU cores and a 32-core Neural Engine. The M5 Ultra supports up to 512GB of unified memory at 1.2TB/s. Apple claims it delivers 4.5 times the peak GPU compute for AI compared to the M3 Ultra and 40 percent faster graphics. The less expensive Mac mini uses the latest 2nm process, while the flagship M5 Ultra remains on the 3nm process used by the M5. This is typical for Ultra chips, which are built from Max dies and usually lag a generation. As a result, the M5 Ultra name does not fully reflect the performance jump it brings, especially for AI workloads. Apple is not planning an M6 Pro or M6 Max, and will move directly to the M7 in mid-2027. Apple's Local AI Push, Mac Clustering, and Higher Prices The machines are aimed less at creators and more at local AI. Apple shipped macOS 26.2 last December with support for low-latency communication between Thunderbolt 5 hosts, specifically for distributed inference using MLX. Since then, hobbyists and developers have been daisy-chaining Mac minis and Studios to run models far larger than a single consumer machine can hold, as an alternative to buying racks. Mac Studio now officially supports clustering over Thunderbolt 5 with RDMA, allowing memory to be pooled across multiple systems. According to Apple, four clustered Studios can deliver up to three times the inference throughput of a single machine. There is also a new Core AI framework in addition to MLX. Apple positions the Studio as its top desktop for on-device AI, while the mini is described as an always-on agentic machine.s-on agentic machine. The economics are simple. Developers using cloud-based coding agents are seeing costs rise, while open-weight models such as Qwen and DeepSeek can do much of the same work on local machines. However, a typical consumer Mac still cannot run models large enough to fully replace advanced APIs, which is why some users have started chaining Macs together. The Mac mini makes up about 3 percent of Mac unit sales in the US, according to Consumer Intelligence Research. The M6 mini starts at $899 and the M5 Pro mini at $1,699, each $100 above the current M4 and M4 Pro models. Mac Studio starts at $2,499 with the M5 Max, the same as the current M4 Max model, and $5,499 with the M5 Ultra. While these comparisons seem to favor Apple, the baseline price has already shifted. The M4 mini launched at $599 in October 2024, but Apple discontinued that version in May, raising the entry price to $799. In late June, Mac prices increased by about 15 to 20 percent, with Tim Cook citing higher component costs as the reason. The lowest-priced Apple desktop is now 50 percent more expensive than it was two months ago, and it still comes with 16GB of memory and a 256GB SSD.ps with 16GB of memory and a 256GB SSD. Upgrades are steep. Another 8GB costs $200, hitting the M6's 32GB ceiling costs $4These price increases are part of a broader industry trend, not unique to Apple. Memory Supply Pressures Behind Apple's Higher Mac Prices DRAM prices rose by about 90 percent quarter over quarter in the first quarter of 2026, and by more than 50 percent again in the second quarter. IDC calls this a structural reallocation of wafer capacity, since wafers used for HBM in AI cannot be used for standard laptop RAM. Microsoft , Asus, MSI, Nintendo, Sony, and Valve have all raised hardware prices this year for similar reasons.us, MSI, Nintendo, Sony, and Valve have all raised hardware prices this year. Demand for the previous Mac mini and Studio models already exceeded supply, with some versions taking weeks or months to ship. Earlier in 2026, Apple removed its largest memory options and has had trouble keeping some MacBook models in stock. The higher memory tiers are now available again on the new mini and Studio, up to 512GB, but that option will not ship until late October. Apple recently highlighted a new Mac mini assembly line in Houston, set to begin production later this year. The company is promoting higher upfront hardware costs as an alternative to ongoing AI service fees, but this only matters if the hardware is actually available. Mac Availability and Apple's Leadership Transition Tim Cook will step down as CEO on August 31, with John Ternus taking over. This makes the new Macs the last products released under Cook's leadership. The upcoming iPhone event in September will be Ternus's first as CEO, where he is expected to introduce what may be Apple's first foldable device and possibly a touchscreen MacBook. Most M6 mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio models will be available on September 22, with preorders already open. The 512GB memory version will not ship until late October. It does not review Macs or AI hardware, so all performance numbers come from Apple and are based on different baselines, including the M1, M4, and M3 Ultra. The main question is whether Apple can keep these new machines in stock, given the ongoing memory supply issues and strong demand seen with the previous generation. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Apple Announces M6 Mac mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio Aimed at Local AI Workloads and Mac Clustering appeared first on gHacks .

The less expensive Mac mini uses the latest 2nm process, while the flagship M5 Ultra remains on the 3nm process used by the M5. This is typical for Ultra chips, which are built from Max dies and usually lag a generation.

As a result, the M5 Ultra name does not fully reflect the performance jump it brings, especially for AI workloads. Apple is not planning an M6 Pro or M6 Max, and will move directly to the M7 in mid-2027.

Apple's Local AI Push, Mac Clustering, and Higher Prices

The machines are aimed less at creators and more at local AI. Apple shipped macOS 26.2 last December with support for low-latency communication between Thunderbolt 5 hosts, specifically for distributed inference using MLX.

Since then, hobbyists and developers have been daisy-chaining Mac minis and Studios to run models far larger than a single consumer machine can hold, as an alternative to buying racks. Mac Studio now officially supports clustering over Thunderbolt 5 with RDMA, allowing memory to be pooled across multiple systems.

According to Apple, four clustered Studios can deliver up to three times the inference throughput of a single machine. There is also a new Core AI framework in addition to MLX. Apple positions the Studio as its top desktop for on-device AI, while the mini is described as an always-on agentic machine.s-on agentic machine.

The economics are simple. Developers using cloud-based coding agents are seeing costs rise, while open-weight models such as Qwen and DeepSeek can do much of the same work on local machines.

However, a typical consumer Mac still cannot run models large enough to fully replace advanced APIs, which is why some users have started chaining Macs together. The Mac mini makes up about 3 percent of Mac unit sales in the US, according to Consumer Intelligence Research.

The M6 mini starts at $899 and the M5 Pro mini at $1,699, each $100 above the current M4 and M4 Pro models. Mac Studio starts at $2,499 with the M5 Max, the same as the current M4 Max model, and $5,499 with the M5 Ultra.

While these comparisons seem to favor Apple, the baseline price has already shifted. The M4 mini launched at $599 in October 2024, but Apple discontinued that version in May, raising the entry price to $799. In late June, Mac prices increased by about 15 to 20 percent, with Tim Cook citing higher component costs as the reason.

The lowest-priced Apple desktop is now 50 percent more expensive than it was two months ago, and it still comes with 16GB of memory and a 256GB SSD.ps with 16GB of memory and a 256GB SSD.

Upgrades are steep. Another 8GB costs $200, hitting the M6's 32GB ceiling costs $4These price increases are part of a broader industry trend, not unique to Apple.

Memory Supply Pressures Behind Apple's Higher Mac Prices

DRAM prices rose by about 90 percent quarter over quarter in the first quarter of 2026, and by more than 50 percent again in the second quarter. IDC calls this a structural reallocation of wafer capacity, since wafers used for HBM in AI cannot be used for standard laptop RAM.

Microsoft, Asus, MSI, Nintendo, Sony, and Valve have all raised hardware prices this year for similar reasons.us, MSI, Nintendo, Sony, and Valve have all raised hardware prices this year.

Demand for the previous Mac mini and Studio models already exceeded supply, with some versions taking weeks or months to ship. Earlier in 2026, Apple removed its largest memory options and has had trouble keeping some MacBook models in stock.

The higher memory tiers are now available again on the new mini and Studio, up to 512GB, but that option will not ship until late October. Apple recently highlighted a new Mac mini assembly line in Houston, set to begin production later this year.

The company is promoting higher upfront hardware costs as an alternative to ongoing AI service fees, but this only matters if the hardware is actually available.

Mac Availability and Apple's Leadership Transition

Tim Cook will step down as CEO on August 31, with John Ternus taking over. This makes the new Macs the last products released under Cook's leadership. The upcoming iPhone event in September will be Ternus's first as CEO, where he is expected to introduce what may be Apple's first foldable device and possibly a touchscreen MacBook.

Most M6 mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio models will be available on September 22, with preorders already open. The 512GB memory version will not ship until late October.

It does not review Macs or AI hardware, so all performance numbers come from Apple and are based on different baselines, including the M1, M4, and M3 Ultra.

The main question is whether Apple can keep these new machines in stock, given the ongoing memory supply issues and strong demand seen with the previous generation.

items.title: 'Shark Tank' star Daniel Lubetzky shares 3 steps to turn a wild idea into a viable business
items.summary: Daniel Lubetzky. Shark Tank Some of the world's wildest ideas sounded implausible before becoming huge businesses. Daniel Lubetzky told Business Insider that founders shouldn't dismiss those ideas too soon. The "Shark Tank" investor shares his 3-step method for moving an idea toward reality. Daniel Lubetzky knows firsthand that great business ideas can sound far-fetched at first. But the "Shark Tank" investor and Kind Snacks founder says entrepreneurs should not dismiss their most outlandish ideas too soon because they're the ones that can turn into some of the most successful businesses. "Out of those crazy things — that's when the Kind bar comes out, the Ring machine that Jamie Siminoff invented — it has to come from the thinking outside of pushing yourself," he said, citing his company's Kind snack bar and the smart-doorbell company acquired by Amazon in 2018 for about $1 billion. The business world is littered with such examples. Airbnb cofounder and CEO Brian Chesky has said people thought it was " crazy " to imagine strangers staying in one another's homes. And Spotify founder Daniel Ek has described the company's original aim — making every song instantly and legally available — as an " impossible idea ." Ahead of the launch of his "Build or Break" podcast on September 3, Lubetzky shared with Business Insider his three-part framework for turning any business idea — no matter how bizarre — from a brainstorm into reality. 1. Be a curious creative "When you're brainstorming, you have to only brainstorm," Lubetzky said. "You have to not allow any filters to apply because it's almost like you need to be looking for the stupidest idea." He said founders should push beyond the obvious options and put every idea on the board, however unrealistic it may initially appear. The goal is to escape conventional thinking , because that is where original concepts can emerge. "The crazier you go, the more you put on your board," he said. "You cannot filter anything out because you have to push yourself outside of that box for you to come up with something that nobody else has ever come up with." 2. Be a consummate critic Then comes the critical stage. After stepping away from the brainstorm, founders should interrogate the ideas that remain with discipline, Lubetzky said. They should consider whether they have the necessary skills, whether customers want the product, whether the economics work, and whether competitors could do it better. "You take a break and then you start applying all of the filters," he said. "Do I have what it takes to do this? Are these the skills that are necessary, and do I have all those skills? Is the input-to-output correlation worth it? Does the consumer really want it? Is there no other competition that can do it better?" This stage requires founders to be tough on their own ideas. "You have to apply 20 filters and ask really tough questions to clean up your brainstorm list and zone in on the thing that's most creative but actually you can pull it off," Lubetzky said. 3. Be a committed crusader Finally, once an entrepreneur has subjected an idea to that "intellectual trial by fire," they need to stop second-guessing themselves and execute, Lubetzky said. "If you still believe that your idea is worth pursuing, once you're ready, you need to switch from being a critic to being a believer," he said. "And you have to just go and execute it no matter what." Lubetzky said the framework applies beyond startups . People can build companies, inventions, schools, or bridges between groups, he said, but they also have a choice in how they use their ideas and energy. "All of us can be builders or destroyers," Lubetzky said. "It's up to us to decide whether we wake up in the morning and try to tear each other apart," or use those tools "to solve problems together." Read the original article on Business Insider

"When you're brainstorming, you have to only brainstorm," Lubetzky said. "You have to not allow any filters to apply because it's almost like you need to be looking for the stupidest idea."

He said founders should push beyond the obvious options and put every idea on the board, however unrealistic it may initially appear. The goal is to escape conventional thinking, because that is where original concepts can emerge.

"The crazier you go, the more you put on your board," he said. "You cannot filter anything out because you have to push yourself outside of that box for you to come up with something that nobody else has ever come up with."

2. Be a consummate critic

Then comes the critical stage.

After stepping away from the brainstorm, founders should interrogate the ideas that remain with discipline, Lubetzky said.

They should consider whether they have the necessary skills, whether customers want the product, whether the economics work, and whether competitors could do it better.

"You take a break and then you start applying all of the filters," he said. "Do I have what it takes to do this? Are these the skills that are necessary, and do I have all those skills? Is the input-to-output correlation worth it? Does the consumer really want it? Is there no other competition that can do it better?"

This stage requires founders to be tough on their own ideas.

"You have to apply 20 filters and ask really tough questions to clean up your brainstorm list and zone in on the thing that's most creative but actually you can pull it off," Lubetzky said.

3. Be a committed crusader

Finally, once an entrepreneur has subjected an idea to that "intellectual trial by fire," they need to stop second-guessing themselves and execute, Lubetzky said.

"If you still believe that your idea is worth pursuing, once you're ready, you need to switch from being a critic to being a believer," he said. "And you have to just go and execute it no matter what."

Lubetzky said the framework applies beyond startups. People can build companies, inventions, schools, or bridges between groups, he said, but they also have a choice in how they use their ideas and energy.

"All of us can be builders or destroyers," Lubetzky said. "It's up to us to decide whether we wake up in the morning and try to tear each other apart," or use those tools "to solve problems together."

items.title: The Witcher 3 Remastered Launches September 29 as a Free Upgrade With Xbox Play Anywhere Support
items.summary: CD Projekt RED has announced The Witcher 3 Remastered. The update arrives on September 29, 2026, as a free upgrade for existing owners. The remaster adds Xbox Play Anywhere support. Players who own The Witcher 3 on GOG, Steam , Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, or Xbox Series X and S will receive the upgrade at no cost. Both major expansions, Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine, are included. The remaster is also available for pre-purchase on Battle.net and Nintendo Switch 2 . The update brings changes to combat, traversal, and visuals, and adds FSR 4.0 support on the Xbox Ally X. The studio has also teased a third expansion for The Witcher 3 and confirmed that The Witcher 4 is planned for 2028. The Witcher 3 Remastered Features and Xbox Play Anywhere Support CD Projekt RED confirmed that the remaster is a free upgrade for existing owners on GOG, Steam, Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and S. Both expansions are included. For those who do not already own the game, it is available for pre-purchase on Battle.net and Nintendo Switch 2. The free update includes a range of changes: Improved combat flow with new finishing moves and skills. Boosted traversal with more dynamic vaulting and platforming. Overhauled visuals with improved lighting and spell effects. Improved monster AI with new enemy moves. Revamped horse riding. A complete Cyberpunk 2077-style overhaul of the skill tree. Armor transmogrification and an improved photo mode. Smaller enhancements include boosted looting, UI interactions, tutorial modernization, and HDR improvements. DLSS 4.5, AMD FSR 4.0, path tracing on high-end systems, and ray-traced hair. CD Projekt RED revealed in the details that the remaster adds Xbox Play Anywhere support, bridging the gap between Xbox Series X and S and Xbox Ally versions. It also gets FSR 4.0 support. The Witcher 3 will also be available on Microsoft and Blizzard's Battle.net. This is part of a broader effort to open Battle.net to third-party developers. More details are expected at BlizzCon 2026 in September. More expected at BlizzCon 2026 in September. Songs of the Past Expansion and Witcher 4 Timeline CD Projekt RED also showed the first teaser trailer for the third and final Witcher 3 DLC, titled "Songs of the Past." The studio described it as a "full-fledged third expansion" that takes Geralt to the peaceful realm of Letten, "where dark secrets lurk beneath the surface," coming in 2027. The trailer features a new hook tool that Geralt uses to pull in enemies, as well as new nature-themed enemies. CD Projekt RED has also confirmed The Witcher 4 is planned for 2028, with the Witcher 3 expansion set for release later in 2027. The Witcher 3 Remastered launches September 29, 2026, as a free upgrade for existing owners on GOG, Steam, Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and S. Pre-purchase is available on Battle.net and Nintendo Switch 2. The "Songs of the Past" expansion is planned for 2027, and The Witcher 4 for 2028, though CD Projekt RED has not provided firm release dates. More information about the Battle.net third-party initiative is expected at BlizzCon 2026 in September. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. items.title: A Canadian premier has 2 ideas on where to hit Trump where it hurts: US fighter jets and coal
items.summary: A Canadian premier says Ottawa should scrap its planned F-35 purchase amid the US trade war. Mateusz Wlodarczyk/NurPhoto/Getty Images A Canadian premier wants Ottawa to look beyond tariffs for ways to hit back at Trump. David Eby says Canada should reconsider buying US F-35 fighter jets as its trade war deepens. Eby also wants Ottawa to consider more taxes on US thermal coal shipped through British Columbia. Canada should broaden its response to its trade war with the US by going beyond tariffs and targeting fighter jets and coal, said a Canadian premier. "I am encouraging the prime minister to look at non-tariff measures to respond, as well, to what the Americans are trying to do to Canadians," British Columbia Premier David Eby said at a press conference on Tuesday. One potential target: Canada's planned purchase of American F-35 fighter jets. "When your friend kicks you in the back, one of the first rules is you don't then go and buy $12 billion of fighter jets from that person," said Eby at a press conference on Tuesday. Canada had planned to acquire 88 F-35s from US defense giant Lockheed Martin, but Carney put the procurement under review shortly after taking office in March 2025. Eby's other potential pressure point is American thermal coal. American thermal coal is shipped through British Columbia to the Westshore terminal near Vancouver, a key export route for US coal producers. Eby said Ottawa should consider additional export tariffs or taxes on those shipments. "We should be having a public discussion," he said. "Should we be buying those fighter jets from the United States? In my opinion, the answer is absolutely not." The proposals come as the US-Canada trade relationship deteriorates sharply. Canada is one of the US's largest trading partners, with about $870 billion in goods and services traded between the two countries in 2025. Trade negotiations broke down last week, and new 50% US tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian imports took effect Saturday. On Monday, Trump also said that tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts, and steel would rise to 50% on January 1. Canada plans dollar-for-dollar retaliation beginning September 8. On Tuesday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne announced tariffs on 27.6 billion Canadian dollars, or about $20 billion, of US imports, including steel, fish, dairy, and electronics. Meanwhile, Carney has highlighted areas where Washington relies on Canada. On Monday, while announcing an $8.2 billion contract for six Canadian Coast Guard icebreakers, Carney pointed to the vessels as an example of one of the "many, many, many things" the US needs from Canada. items.title: FedEx’s Robot Playbook: Rent the Arms, Own the Network
items.summary: FedEx and Dexterity just expanded their robotic trailer-loading program at the FedEx Hagerstown Hub in Maryland, moving the system beyond its original pilot site. On the surface, it looks like routine automation news. Underneath, it reveals a strategic choice that separates FedEx from Amazon and could decide which logistics giant scales automation faster over the next five years. What FedEx and Dexterity Actually Announced FedEx and Dexterity announced the expanded deployment on July 30, 2026, scaling Dexterity’s Foresight world model and Mech trailer-loading system at Hagerstown. Foresight combines vision, depth, and touch to reason across three spatial dimensions and time, deciding in real time how to place packages for space, stability, and speed. The deployment follows several years of joint development and testing at a smaller pilot site, and it moves the technology into production at a meaningfully larger scale. FedEx says it will also use the Hagerstown rollout to study how the robots affect destination planning, trailer assignments, maintenance schedules, and workforce processes across the hub. Neither company disclosed how many robots will run at Hagerstown or offered a timeline for expanding to other hubs. FedEx did tell investors at its 2026 Investor Day that it intends to scale trailer loading and unloading across multiple U.S. hubs in the coming years. The Real Strategy Is Refusing to Build Robots In-House The more interesting story sits one layer up. FedEx has deliberately chosen not to build a proprietary robotics stack the way Amazon has. Instead, it runs a portfolio of point solutions from outside vendors: Dexterity handles trailer loading, Berkshire Grey’s Scoop bot handles bulk unloading, and the company has previously worked with fulfillment robotics startup Nimble. Stephanie Cook, FedEx’s director of advanced technology and innovation for robotics, told TechCrunch that building this kind of system in-house wasn’t realistic. “We knew it wasn’t something that we could just develop in a matter of months. It was going to take a multi-year journey to get here,” she said of the Berkshire Grey partnership, a description that applies just as well to the Dexterity relationship. O.P. Skaaksrud, FedEx’s vice president of advanced technology and innovation, framed the logic even more directly in the same interview, arguing that hardware isn’t where FedEx’s real advantage sits. Trucks are just trucks, in his view. The network and software behind FedEx’s delivery system are what make FedEx, FedEx. That’s a variation on a familiar strategic pattern: let outside vendors compete on hardware, and keep the coordinating layer, the actual moat, in-house. This isn’t FedEx’s first attempt at robotics, and the earlier misses explain the current caution. Its SameDay Bot last-mile delivery robot, launched in 2019, was pulled from New York City sidewalks under then-mayor Bill de Blasio within its first year. FedEx also ended its multiyear partnership with autonomous delivery company Nuro after Nuro shifted its business model away from delivery robots toward licensing its self-driving technology in 2025. Spreading bets across several vendors, rather than committing fully to one, looks less like indecision and more like a company that has already been burned by picking a single partner too early. Dexterity Isn’t FedEx’s Only Option, and That’s the Point Dexterity was last valued at $1.65 billion following a $95 million round in March 2025 led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Sumitomo Corporation, one of its largest customers. Sumitomo has committed to deploying 1,500 Dexterity robots across Japanese warehouses by 2026, giving the startup a second large anchor customer beyond FedEx. But Dexterity isn’t operating in a vacuum. Boston Dynamics’ Stretch, Pickle Robot’s Pickle Unload System, and Anyware Robotics’ Pixmo all compete for the same trailer-loading and unloading contracts. That competitive field matters more than it might seem: it means FedEx can keep leverage over pricing and performance without locking itself into a single robotics supplier, the same optionality that shaped its earlier partnership decisions. What This Means for the Rest of Logistics FedEx’s caution about announcing scale, no robot counts, no rollout timeline, tells its own story. This isn’t a company that has solved the economics of warehouse automation and is now racing to deploy. It’s a company still validating unit economics hub by hub before committing capital. That pace sits uneasily next to FedEx’s broader network math: the company closed 93 buildings in 2025 and has flagged at least 24 more closures for the first half of 2026, even as it credits automation and network efficiency with helping it deliver more than 40% of shipments same-day or overnight in the first half of the year. FedEx has not linked the closures directly to robotics, and the two trends may simply share a common driver in cost discipline. But warehouse employees watching robots arrive at a hub that’s also shedding buildings elsewhere have a reasonable basis for asking how the two trends fit together. Expect FedEx to keep expanding this multi-vendor approach hub by hub rather than betting on one robotics supplier. The strategy trades a proprietary moat for speed and negotiating leverage, and it has already gotten Dexterity’s system to production scale faster than a fully in-house program likely would have. Whether that trade holds up the next time FedEx faces a cost-cutting cycle will say as much about the company’s operating discipline as it does about the robots themselves. items.title: IBM Releases Granite 4.2: Bringing Native Reasoning and Agentic RL to Open Enterprise Models
items.summary: IBM has released Granite 4.2 , a family of open reasoning language models in 3B, 8B, and 30B parameter sizes. Unlike earlier Granite releases, which were instruction-following assistants, Granite 4.2 is built around explicit reasoning. Every model can emit a chain of thought before answering, and every model exposes a thinking / non-thinking switch plus a low-effort mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions. The models are decoder-only dense transformers, pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15 trillion tokens, then post-trained through a multi-stage reinforcement learning chain. For the 8B and 30B, that chain includes an agentic RL block where the model learns to edit code, drive a terminal, and run web searches inside real sandboxed environments. All three ship under Apache 2.0 . IBM also released two 470M-parameter Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC models alongside the LLMs. Is it deployable? Yes, All three Granite 4.2 language models ship under Apache 2.0 , so download, fine-tuning, and commercial production use carry no licensing gate. Which companies : The 3B fits solo developers and startups running on a laptop through Ollama or LM Studio , especially with the released GGUF quants down to Q4_K_M. The 8B suits mid-market teams on a single modern GPU. The 30B targets enterprises with A100/H100-class capacity, or FP8/NVFP4 serving on vLLM . Regulated organizations get the additional benefit of on-prem weights. Industries : Software and developer tooling, financial services, healthcare, telecom, public sector, and contact centers, which is where the new speech models land. Applications : Software engineering agents, terminal and DevOps automation, deep-research and search agents, long-document RAG, structured tool calling, and high-volume transcription. Architecture Granite 4.2 is a decoder-only dense transformer, not a hybrid or MoE design. Core components are Grouped Query Attention with 8 KV heads, RoPE with θ = 10,000,000, SwiGLU MLPs, RMSNorm (ε = 1e-5), untied input/output embeddings, and bfloat16 precision. The 3B uses 40 layers at embedding size 2560. The 8B uses 40 layers at 4096. The 30B goes to 64 layers with an MLP hidden size of 32,768. The published architecture table lists a 131,072-token (128K) sequence length , while the five-phase pre-training run includes a long-context phase extending to 512K tokens. Pre-training covers roughly 15 trillion tokens from scratch. The training pipeline is the actual story Supervised fine-tuning uses about 7.2 million samples , roughly 100B tokens with ~65B trainable. The mixture is 31.6% agentic and 68.4% non-agentic , and software engineering is 69% of the agentic slice. Trajectories were generated across harnesses including OpenHands, SWE-agent, Terminus-2, MiniSWE, Codex, and Goose. Quality control used GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as judges, plus SHA-256 deduplication over the tools and messages fields. Post-training is a multi-stage, multi-environment RL chain , not a single pass. Each stage is a separate asynchronous GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint, with a leave-one-out baseline instead of a value network and truncated importance sampling to bound off-policy drift. The order is RLVR, then skill boosters, then SWE, Terminal, Search, then RLHF. The agentic RL block runs only on the 8B and 30B . The 3B takes foundational RL and alignment only. That single design choice explains most of the capability gap across sizes. Training ran on NeMo-RL and NeMo-Gym over an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave. Two supporting pieces matter: 1 trillion tokens of synthetic code from IBM’s CodeAlchemy pipeline, and a speculative decoding layer for faster serving. Reported results IBM’s numbers, by size (3B / 8B / 30B): Benchmark 3B 8B 30B SWE-Bench Verified NA 47.67 57.00 Terminal-Bench 2.1 NA 20.56 29.24 τ³-bench 50.99 66.34 68.05 BFCL (v4) 52.41 50.29 61.39 AIME25 78.33 86.67 89.17 GPQA 54.80 64.14 66.41 MMLU-Pro 67.84 74.04 77.60 RULER 128K 55.30 71.41 81.38 Speech: 470M parameters, no LLM backbone The Turbo CTC models come in at 470 million parameters and drop the LLM backbone entirely, using connectionist temporal classification to map audio to text. IBM reports an RTFx throughput near 12,600 on a single H200 , against roughly 6,000 for current speed leaders on the Open ASR leaderboard . A WebGPU demo is live. Key Takeaways Granite 4.2 ships dense 3B/8B/30B reasoning models under Apache 2.0. A thinking / low-effort / non-thinking switch is exposed in the chat template. Agentic RL (SWE, Terminal, Search) trains only the 8B and 30B. The 30B hits 57.00 on SWE-Bench Verified and 29.24 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC is 470M parameters with no LLM backbone. Check out the IBM Research blog , the technical write-up , and the GitHub repo . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. IBM has released Granite 4.2, a family of open reasoning language models in 3B, 8B, and 30B parameter sizes. Unlike earlier Granite releases, which were instruction-following assistants, Granite 4.2 is built around explicit reasoning. Every model can emit a chain of thought before answering, and every model exposes a thinking / non-thinking switch plus a low-effort mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions. The models are decoder-only dense transformers, pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15 trillion tokens, then post-trained through a multi-stage reinforcement learning chain. For the 8B and 30B, that chain includes an agentic RL block where the model learns to edit code, drive a terminal, and run web searches inside real sandboxed environments. All three ship under Apache 2.0. IBM also released two 470M-parameter Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC models alongside the LLMs.

Is it deployable?

Yes, All three Granite 4.2 language models ship under Apache 2.0, so download, fine-tuning, and commercial production use carry no licensing gate.

  • Which companies: The 3B fits solo developers and startups running on a laptop through Ollama or LM Studio, especially with the released GGUF quants down to Q4_K_M. The 8B suits mid-market teams on a single modern GPU. The 30B targets enterprises with A100/H100-class capacity, or FP8/NVFP4 serving on vLLM. Regulated organizations get the additional benefit of on-prem weights.
  • Industries: Software and developer tooling, financial services, healthcare, telecom, public sector, and contact centers, which is where the new speech models land.
  • Applications: Software engineering agents, terminal and DevOps automation, deep-research and search agents, long-document RAG, structured tool calling, and high-volume transcription.
Architecture

Granite 4.2 is a decoder-only dense transformer, not a hybrid or MoE design. Core components are Grouped Query Attention with 8 KV heads, RoPE with θ = 10,000,000, SwiGLU MLPs, RMSNorm (ε = 1e-5), untied input/output embeddings, and bfloat16 precision.

The 3B uses 40 layers at embedding size 2560. The 8B uses 40 layers at 4096. The 30B goes to 64 layers with an MLP hidden size of 32,768. The published architecture table lists a 131,072-token (128K) sequence length, while the five-phase pre-training run includes a long-context phase extending to 512K tokens. Pre-training covers roughly 15 trillion tokens from scratch.

The training pipeline is the actual story

Supervised fine-tuning uses about 7.2 million samples, roughly 100B tokens with ~65B trainable. The mixture is 31.6% agentic and 68.4% non-agentic, and software engineering is 69% of the agentic slice. Trajectories were generated across harnesses including OpenHands, SWE-agent, Terminus-2, MiniSWE, Codex, and Goose. Quality control used GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as judges, plus SHA-256 deduplication over the tools and messages fields.

Post-training is a multi-stage, multi-environment RL chain, not a single pass. Each stage is a separate asynchronous GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint, with a leave-one-out baseline instead of a value network and truncated importance sampling to bound off-policy drift. The order is RLVR, then skill boosters, then SWE, Terminal, Search, then RLHF.

The agentic RL block runs only on the 8B and 30B. The 3B takes foundational RL and alignment only. That single design choice explains most of the capability gap across sizes. Training ran on NeMo-RL and NeMo-Gym over an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave.

Two supporting pieces matter: 1 trillion tokens of synthetic code from IBM’s CodeAlchemy pipeline, and a speculative decoding layer for faster serving.

Reported results

IBM’s numbers, by size (3B / 8B / 30B):

  • A thinking / low-effort / non-thinking switch is exposed in the chat template.

items.title: Canadian politicians say Trump can rename that lake whatever he likes, but it'll 'always be Lake Ontario'
items.summary: Canadian politicians aren't too concerned about Trump's threat to rename Lake Ontario. Arrush Chopra/NurPhoto via Getty Images Canada's leaders heard Trump's threat to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, and they don't really care. They said it will always be Lake Ontario in Canada, regardless of what Trump decides to name it. Trump's threat comes as yet another trade war is erupting between the two neighbors. Canadian politicians say President Donald Trump can rename Lake Ontario on the map if he wants to — it won't change what they call it. In a Tuesday morning Truth Social post, Trump wrote that the US is "giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America" as "we don't expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer." He later posted a picture of the map of Lake Ontario with its name crossed out and replaced by "Lake America" in a bold metallic font. His threat comes as trade tensions between the two countries flare. But Canadian politicians shrugged off Trump's message. Talking about Trump, Ontario Premier Doug Ford told CBS News on Tuesday: "I have to laugh when he comes up with these ideas." "It's always going to be Lake Ontario here in Canada. And, you know, that's up to the president," Ford added. "If he wants to name it Lake America, Lake Trump, whatever he wants to do, that's his prerogative." Canada's Minister of Industry, Mélanie Joly, said in a Tuesday presser, "We'll always call it Lake Ontario. Period." "We'll just stand up for what we have. Canadian politicians aren't too concerned about Trump's threat to rename Lake Ontario.

Arrush Chopra/NurPhoto via Getty Images

  • Canada's leaders heard Trump's threat to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, and they don't really care.

Canadian politicians say President Donald Trump can rename Lake Ontario on the map if he wants to — it won't change what they call it.

In a Tuesday morning Truth Social post, Trump wrote that the US is "giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America" as "we don't expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer."

Talking about Trump, Ontario Premier Doug Ford told CBS News on Tuesday: "I have to laugh when he comes up with these ideas."

items.title: Your Computer Is a Garrison. It Needs a Staff Officer
items.summary: I built a dashboard to run every project on my machine. Then I spent far longer making it run on anyone else’s. GSO-1 / V0.1.0 / APACHE-2.0 There are thirty-odd folders in my projects directory. Four of them are running right now and I am not completely certain which four. Two are on a branch I abandoned in March. One is holding port 3000 hostage and I will find out which one by killing things until the error goes away. Starting any of them means remembering whether it was npm run dev, ./run.sh, uvicorn app:app --reload, or that one make serve I wrote in 2023 and have never typed since. This is not a hard problem. It is a staff problem. And armies solved it a century ago. FIG. 1 The GSO-1 site The name is the whole design In a division headquarters there is an officer called the GSO-1 : General Staff Officer Grade 1, a Lieutenant Colonel who heads the General Staff branch. He is the right hand of the GOC , the General Officer Commanding the division. He plans the operations, keeps the picture current, and drafts the orders the commander signs. Below him sit the GSO-2, a Major, and the GSO-3, a Captain. In peace and in war, the division runs through him. He works from the Ops Room , the nerve centre where the maps, the traces, the unit locations, the strengths and the intelligence are all displayed and kept up to date. It is where the commander is briefed, and where decisions actually get made, because it is the one place the whole situation can be seen at once. Here is the move: your computer is your garrison, and you are its GOC. You decide what gets built and what ships. You should not also be the person tracking which of thirty services is currently up. That is staff work. It always was. So I built the staff officer, and I called it GSO-1, and the screen it works from is the Ops Room. I want to be careful here, because software people love a metaphor and most of them are decoration. This one isn’t. It made specific decisions for me, and I can show you which. FIG 2: The Ops Room dashboard A 1960s staff manual is a surprisingly good product spec While building this I went looking for what the old British Army manuals actually say a General Staff Officer is for . A 1964 document titled Hints to General Staff Officers turns out to read like a design review. Four principles from it, and what each one changed in the software: “Serve the commander wisely and well.” The tool’s job is to know things so you don’t have to. GSO-1 walks every project, works out how each one starts, and gives you a start button. It detects Node, Django, FastAPI, Flask, Streamlit, Rust, Go, static sites and plain Python. And it always defers to a project’s own run.sh or Makefile over its own guess. An explicit instruction from the unit beats staff inference. Always. “Stay largely invisible; the commander gets the credit.” GSO-1 has no opinions about how you build software. It does not want to be your framework, your runtime, or your workflow. It starts what you already built, in the way you already built it, and then it gets out of the way. There is no GSO-1 config format to learn. There is one environment variable most people ever touch. “Shield the commander from unnecessary detail, reserving him for the important decisions.” This is the whole home screen. Thirty repos, and the Ops Room leads with the four that actually need you: the dirty ones, the stale ones, the one that crashed, the one holding a port. Everything else is one click away and silent until it isn’t. “Never be a ‘yes man’.” A staff officer who only reports good news is worse than having no staff officer, because now you’re confidently wrong. So GSO-1 shows the crashed process, the failed run, and the port conflict plainly, in red, on the first screen, in the same band as everything that is fine. A dashboard that is always green is a dashboard nobody checks. What it actually does FIG. 3 One question on first run, then it gets out of the way. Point it at a folder. It lists everything inside, works out how each project starts, and gives you a row per app with a start button, a live health light, and the git state. Start and stop anything , without remembering how. Each app runs in its own process group; logs stream to a file per app. Real health , not hope: process tracking plus a port probe, reporting healthy, starting, crashed or stopped. Port conflicts found before launch , rather than after the stack trace. Git at a glance across every repo, branch, dirty count, ahead/behind, last commit, with fast-forward updates from the dashboard. Multiple roots , so your personal projects and your work checkouts each get their own tab. Agents with a seatbelt. GSO-1 can drive a claude CLI session inside any project it manages. Read-only tools run themselves; anything that writes a file or runs a command stops for an explicit Allow or Deny. Your own hardware. A built-in Anthropic→llama proxy points an agent session at your local llama-server, so the whole session can run on your GPU. It binds to 127.0.0.1 by default and uploads nothing. It is a control plane for a machine you already own. FIG. 4 The companion at /m, behind a token you set on purpose. The part nobody warns you about Everything above took a while, but it was the fun kind of while. Then I decided to let other people install it, and discovered that I had not built an application. I had built a checkout. This is the part I actually want to tell you about, because I don’t think it’s specific to my project at all. Five ways a tool says “this only runs on my machine” I went looking for everything that assumed it was running on my laptop. I found five, and none of them would have thrown an error during development, because during development every one of those assumptions was true. 1. A hardcoded home directory. The dashboard abbreviated long paths to ~/… by comparing against a string literal of my own home directory. On anyone else's machine, paths just silently rendered in full. The fix is dull, the server reports the real home directory and the UI uses that, but the interesting part is that this bug is invisible to its author by construction . 2. An identity in the markup. The greeting, the sidebar card, and both avatars had my name typed into the HTML. It now comes from the OS account record. One detail worth stealing: I take the whole name rather than the first word, because splitting on the first token greets “MD Rafsun Sheikh” as “MD”, and every rule you write for detecting a name prefix is wrong for somebody. 3. State written inside the application directory. The registry, logs and scheduler state all lived in /data. That is perfectly fine for a checkout and completely broken for a packaged app, where the bundle is read-only on macOS and lives in Program Files on Windows. State now resolves per platform (Application Support, %APPDATA%, XDG_DATA_HOME) and stays beside the code in a source checkout so existing installs don't lose anything. 4. A default pointing at my own stuff. The site CMS module defaulted to a specific Jekyll checkout, my personal blog, and named it in the module docstring. There is no sensible default for “which of your repositories is your blog”, so there no longer is one: the feature stays switched off until an environment variable names a real checkout. 5. A security-relevant default that was also a personal path. The agent sidecar’s sandbox root, the only directory the agent is allowed to write to , defaulted to a fixed path under my home directory. On any other machine that names a directory that does not exist. It now resolves from the sidecar’s own install location. This is the one that bothered me most, because it was a wrong default in a security boundary, and it was wrong in the quiet direction. If you take one thing from this section: grep your own source for your own username before you publish anything. I added it to CI, so the build now fails on any /Users/ or /home/ path in the codebase. The first thing that lint caught was a comment I had written in the commit that introduced the lint. Freezing a Python server into something people can double-click The backend is FastAPI and uvicorn. The desktop shell is Electron. The requirement was that a user needs no Python at all. PyInstaller does this, with one caveat worth knowing: uvicorn and FastAPI resolve a lot of their machinery by string at runtime , so static analysis misses it and you get a binary that builds cleanly and then dies on boot. Collecting the packages wholesale via collect_submodules is the reliable fix. The result is a self-contained server of about 34 MB that carries the dashboard's static files inside the bundle. Electron then ships that binary as an extra resource. When the app detects it is packaged, it spawns the bundled server directly and points its state at the per-user data directory. When it is running from a checkout, it takes the original development path unchanged, so npm start in the repo behaves exactly as it always did. Two modes, one shell, and the dev experience is not sacrificed to the packaging. The hard requirement I set was that quitting must leave no orphans. The server runs in its own process group and gets signalled on the way out, so closing the window can never leave a headless uvicorn holding the port. Windows gets its own shutdown path, because there are no process groups there to signal. The first-run question A packaged application arrives on a machine knowing nothing about it. The one thing GSO-1 genuinely cannot guess is where you keep your code. So there is exactly one first-run screen: pick the folder. Browse it, or type a path, or add several roots. It is not dismissible, because there is no dashboard behind it until a folder is chosen. Two small decisions in there I’d defend: The screen is styled with inline styles rather than the app’s utility classes. The stylesheet is a purged Tailwind build that gets regenerated by hand, and the one screen a fresh install absolutely must render correctly cannot depend on a build artefact being current. And an unreadable folder offers you Home and / as a way back, rather than reporting failure and stranding you on the one screen you're not allowed to skip. My first version just printed an error. That is a dead end on the very first thing a new user sees. FIG. 5 Six projects, six stacks: node, script, static, python, go, rust. It worked out the kind on its own. Four CI failures, none of them my code Tagging the release and watching it fail on all platforms, four times, in four different ways: The PyInstaller spec used working-directory-relative paths. I built it from inside build/, CI builds from the repo root, so pathex=[".."] resolved to the parent of the checkout. PyInstaller cheerfully produced a binary with no application on its path, which then failed at startup rather than at build time. Everything is anchored to the spec's own location now. electron-builder was told to publish and told not to. The build step exported GH_TOKEN, which is enough for electron-builder to infer a GitHub publish provider and start assembling auto-update metadata, which then dereferences a publish config that --publish never never built: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'channel') at computeChannelNames (updateInfoBuilder.ts) The token was never needed; the release is assembled from uploaded artifacts in a separate job. I reproduced this locally with the token set before changing anything. The fix then took two minutes. The reproduction is what made it a fix rather than a guess, and I’d recommend it as a general habit. The .deb target requires an author email. The manifest only had a name. Easy, but it fails the whole Linux job. The macOS Intel job never failed at all, it queued forever. GitHub has retired the macos-13 Intel runners, so a job pinned to them waits for a machine that is not coming. This one cost the most wall-clock time precisely because it wasn't an error. A single Apple Silicon runner cross-builds both architectures, which is what the local build had been doing all along. Then it went green, and it has been green since. A note on what this thing can do GSO-1 starts processes and runs commands as you. That is the entire feature set, and it is also the threat model. Anyone who can reach its port can run code as you. So: loopback only by default, unreachable from the network. Remote access refused outright unless you set a token. Agent writes and commands require explicit approval. While auditing before release I found a real one. The remote-auth allowlist matched public paths with startswith, so the prefix /m, the phone companion, would also have matched a future /models or /metrics, exposing them to the network without a token. Nothing exposed at the time actually collided, so nothing was reachable. But the gate was one route name away from opening, and the next person to add a top-level endpoint would never have known. Prefixes now match on a path boundary, verified across eighteen cases. I mention it because “no vulnerability was exploitable” and “the design was safe” are different statements, and only the first one was true. If you’re about to ship your own tool The generalisable parts, as briefly as I can put them: Your dev environment is a set of assumptions, not a baseline. Every one of my five portability bugs was true-by-construction on my machine and therefore invisible. Lint for your own identity. Username, home directory, personal repos, employer paths. Make CI fail on it. It will catch you at least once. A packaged app cannot write where it lives. Decide where state goes before you package, not after. Reproduce build failures locally before fixing them. Every one of my CI fixes took minutes once reproduced and would have been guesswork otherwise. Ship the failure states in your screenshots. A dashboard that is always green teaches people not to look at it. Get it GSO-1 is Apache-2.0 and installs on macOS, Windows and Linux. On first run it asks which folder holds your projects. That is the entire setup: no Python, no terminal, no config file. Download: github.com/rafsunsheikh/gso-1/releases Source: github.com/rafsunsheikh/gso-1 Site: rafsunsheikh.github.io/gso-1 Current builds are unsigned, so macOS and Windows will ask you to allow the app once. If GSO-1 guesses the wrong run command for your stack, that is the single easiest pull request in the repository, and I would genuinely like to have it. Your computer is your garrison. You shouldn’t have to do the staff work too. Sources and honest limits The military background is drawn from published descriptions of the British and Commonwealth staff system, the GSO-1’s role at division headquarters, the GSO-2/GSO-3 structure beneath it, and the function of an operations room as the place where the current picture is maintained and the commander is briefed. The four principles quoted are from Hints to General Staff Officers (1964), which is available online. I am describing a staff system as documented, not claiming personal military service. Figures in this article that you can check yourself: the repository is 45 commits and 105 tracked files; the backend is roughly 6,700 lines of Python and the agent sidecar about 1,500 lines of TypeScript; the published installers are 112 to 156 MB depending on platform. The frozen backend size of “about 34 MB” is a measurement from my own build machine and will vary with platform and Python version. The four CI failures are each traceable to the commit that fixed them. Disclaimer: While building the application, I took the opportunity to use Vibe coding. And yes, writing this article, I took help from Generative AI. Why riding horse, when cars are already on the road? Although, it matters who is behind the wheel, right? Your Computer Is a Garrison. It Needs a Staff Officer was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

The .deb target requires an author email. The manifest only had a name. Easy, but it fails the whole Linux job.

The macOS Intel job never failed at all, it queued forever. GitHub has retired the macos-13 Intel runners, so a job pinned to them waits for a machine that is not coming. This one cost the most wall-clock time precisely because it wasn't an error. A single Apple Silicon runner cross-builds both architectures, which is what the local build had been doing all along.

Then it went green, and it has been green since.

A note on what this thing can do

GSO-1 starts processes and runs commands as you. That is the entire feature set, and it is also the threat model. Anyone who can reach its port can run code as you.

So: loopback only by default, unreachable from the network. Remote access refused outright unless you set a token. Agent writes and commands require explicit approval.

While auditing before release I found a real one. The remote-auth allowlist matched public paths with startswith, so the prefix /m, the phone companion, would also have matched a future /models or /metrics, exposing them to the network without a token. Nothing exposed at the time actually collided, so nothing was reachable. But the gate was one route name away from opening, and the next person to add a top-level endpoint would never have known. Prefixes now match on a path boundary, verified across eighteen cases.

I mention it because “no vulnerability was exploitable” and “the design was safe” are different statements, and only the first one was true.

If you’re about to ship your own tool

The generalisable parts, as briefly as I can put them:

  • Your dev environment is a set of assumptions, not a baseline. Every one of my five portability bugs was true-by-construction on my machine and therefore invisible.
  • Lint for your own identity. Username, home directory, personal repos, employer paths. Make CI fail on it. It will catch you at least once.
  • A packaged app cannot write where it lives. Decide where state goes before you package, not after.
  • Reproduce build failures locally before fixing them. Every one of my CI fixes took minutes once reproduced and would have been guesswork otherwise.
  • Ship the failure states in your screenshots. A dashboard that is always green teaches people not to look at it.
Get it

GSO-1 is Apache-2.0 and installs on macOS, Windows and Linux. On first run it asks which folder holds your projects. That is the entire setup: no Python, no terminal, no config file.

  • Download: github.com/rafsunsheikh/gso-1/releases
  • Source: github.com/rafsunsheikh/gso-1
  • Site: rafsunsheikh.github.io/gso-1

Current builds are unsigned, so macOS and Windows will ask you to allow the app once. If GSO-1 guesses the wrong run command for your stack, that is the single easiest pull request in the repository, and I would genuinely like to have it.

Your computer is your garrison. You shouldn’t have to do the staff work too.

Sources and honest limits

The military background is drawn from published descriptions of the British and Commonwealth staff system, the GSO-1’s role at division headquarters, the GSO-2/GSO-3 structure beneath it, and the function of an operations room as the place where the current picture is maintained and the commander is briefed. The four principles quoted are from Hints to General Staff Officers (1964), which is available online. I am describing a staff system as documented, not claiming personal military service.

Figures in this article that you can check yourself: the repository is 45 commits and 105 tracked files; the backend is roughly 6,700 lines of Python and the agent sidecar about 1,500 lines of TypeScript; the published installers are 112 to 156 MB depending on platform. The frozen backend size of “about 34 MB” is a measurement from my own build machine and will vary with platform and Python version. The four CI failures are each traceable to the commit that fixed them.

Disclaimer: While building the application, I took the opportunity to use Vibe coding. And yes, writing this article, I took help from Generative AI. Why riding horse, when cars are already on the road? Although, it matters who is behind the wheel, right?
